Permintaan daftar nama mahasiswa membutu:
A request for a list of student names requires two decisions: the table that stores students and the column that stores their names. SELECT and FROM express those two decisions. Reading data does not modify the source records.

## FROM: choose the source

The question determines the type of fact needed. A list of courses comes from courses; a list of students comes from students. FROM specifies the source table.

## SELECT: choose the columns

SELECT specifies the result columns. `SELECT course_code, course_name FROM courses;` selects two attributes. `SELECT * FROM courses;` helps with initial inspection but displays all columns. The column order in SELECT becomes the column order of the result.

## A result shape you can explain

The query result is a new table to read, not a transfer of the source records. Without ORDER BY, row order is not guaranteed. The examples use ORDER BY course_id so that exercise results are stable; ordering is covered in the next material.

```sql
SELECT course_code, course_name
FROM courses
ORDER BY course_id;
```

## Example reading

```sql
SELECT student_id, name
FROM students
ORDER BY student_id;
```

The result contains the `student_id` and `name` columns. The `cohort` column remains stored in students, but it is not selected for this result. The column order follows the SELECT list. ORDER BY only makes the display order clearer.

`SELECT *` selects all columns. For specific information needs, an explicit column list is easier to check. Choosing the wrong source table cannot be fixed just by renaming columns.

## Summary

FROM sets the source of records and SELECT picks the result columns. A read query produces a representation of the data without changing the source table.

The two highest values can only be selected correctly if the results are sorted first. Sorting determines the position of records in the results, while limiting determines the number of records displayed.

## ASC and DESC

ORDER BY sorts the results; it does not change the storage order of records. ASC means ascending; DESC descending. Different values in enrollments.score help make the impact clearly visible.

## Tied values and tie-breakers

If the sort column values are equal, use a second column to determine the order. All courses have credits 3. `ORDER BY credits DESC, course_name ASC` sorts the names when credits are tied.

## LIMIT after sorting

LIMIT restricts the number of results. For the two highest values, sort by score DESC, use enrollment_id as the tie-breaker, then LIMIT 2.

```sql
SELECT enrollment_id, score
FROM enrollments
ORDER BY score DESC, enrollment_id ASC
LIMIT 2;
```

## Example results of the two highest values

| enrollment_id | score |
| --- | --- |
| 6 | 95 |
| 1 | 88 |

Those results come from score in descending order. When two records have the same score, ascending enrollment_id becomes a consistent tie-breaker. Without ORDER BY, the database does not guarantee the order of results; an order you once saw is not a rule you can rely on.

## Summary

ASC sorts ascending and DESC descending. A tie-breaker column resolves tied values. LIMIT takes a number of records from the already sorted results, without removing the source records.

Ringkasan menjawab pertanyaan tentang se:
Summaries answer questions about a set of records: how many registrations there are and what their average score is. A single summary result row can represent many source records, so the unit being counted must be clear.

## COUNT counts records

COUNT(*) counts the source result rows. In this dataset each enrollment is one registration. Do not equate the number of enrollments with the number of unique students: Alya and Bima each have two enrollments.

## GROUP BY forms groups

GROUP BY course_id summarizes registrations per course. Take course 10: its group members are enrollments #1, #3, and #6. COUNT for that group reads three records, not the number of columns or the number of credits.

```sql
SELECT course_id, COUNT(*) AS participants
FROM enrollments
GROUP BY course_id
ORDER BY course_id;
```

## AVG and one row per group

AVG(score) computes the average score of the group members. For course 10, (88 + 74 + 95) / 3 ≈ 85.67. ROUND(..., 2) rounds the number; the displays 85 and 85.00 have the same value. JOIN adds the course name; GROUP BY still determines one row per course that has enrollments.

## Example score summary

```sql
SELECT course_id, COUNT(*) AS participants,
       ROUND(AVG(score), 2) AS average_score
FROM enrollments
GROUP BY course_id
ORDER BY course_id;
```

COUNT(*) counts all records in the group. AVG(score) computes the average of the non-NULL scores; the two do not always use the same count if there are empty values. The example dataset has all scores filled in. Columns selected outside aggregate functions should also determine the grouping, so that the meaning of each row is clear.

## Summary

COUNT counts records, AVG summarizes scores, and GROUP BY defines the groups. The number of registrations is not automatically the number of unique students.

Laporan jumlah peserta dengan nilai mini:
A report of the number of participants with a minimum score of 85 per course combines source selection, table relationships, filtering, grouping, and ordering. Each part of the query answers a different part of the information need.

## Translate the request into data

Scores are in enrollments, course names in courses. Use the course_id relationship to join them. This question does not need students because student names are not requested.

## Filter before summarizing

WHERE score >= 85 selects enrollments before GROUP BY forms groups. The average only uses records that pass, not all participants. Displaying the same course name does not mean the group still contains the same records.

## Check the results, not just that the query runs

Use COUNT and AVG, sort the average in descending order, and use the name as a tiebreaker when scores are tied. A wrong JOIN can produce results that look plausible but come from the wrong pairs.

## Example of an integrated report

```sql
SELECT c.course_name, COUNT(*) AS participants,
       ROUND(AVG(e.score), 2) AS average_score
FROM enrollments AS e
JOIN courses AS c ON c.course_id = e.course_id
WHERE e.score >= 85
GROUP BY c.course_id, c.course_name
ORDER BY average_score DESC, c.course_name ASC;
```

Conceptually, the source and relationship pairs determine the records, WHERE limits which records are read, GROUP BY forms groups, aggregates produce the summary, and ORDER BY sorts the results. This is a model for reasoning about queries, not a guarantee of the database engine's internal order of operations.

For course 10, the score 74 does not pass the 85 threshold, so the group only uses 88 and 95. The count is two and the average is 91.5. Lowering the threshold can add group members and change the average.

## Summary

Query correctness is determined by the meaning of the source, key pairs, conditions, groups, and results. Accepted syntax does not yet guarantee the answer meets the need.

The score of enrollment number 3 was originally 74 and needs to be corrected to 78. UPDATE changes values in an existing record. The enrollment identity and the number of records stay the same; only the attributes set in SET change.

## Find one target

Start with `SELECT * FROM enrollments WHERE enrollment_id = 3;`. Bima has two enrollments; student_id 2 is not a narrow enough target. The PK enrollment_id identifies a single record.

## SET for values, WHERE for the target

SET specifies the new attributes; WHERE specifies the record that receives the change.

```sql
UPDATE enrollments
SET score = 78
WHERE enrollment_id = 3;
```

Without WHERE, every record could change on a regular database; the lab deliberately rejects it. Do not rely on the lab's rejection as a substitute for the habit of choosing a target.

## Before and after evidence

The Preview shows score 74 → 78 without saving the change right away. Confirm only when the record and value are correct. The local object changes once applied; enrollment record #4 remains 82. Use SELECT with the same predicate to verify.

## State before and after

| enrollment_id | Score before | Score after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 3 | 74 | 78 |
| 4 | 82 | 82 |

A WHERE that uses student_id can hit multiple enrollments of the same student. The enrollment identity is more precise when only one value needs correcting. Safe changes start from a target you can explain, not from the assumption that every record in the table must receive a new value.

## Summary

UPDATE changes attributes of an existing record. SET states the new value and WHERE states the target. The number of records stays the same; verification ensures other records did not change along with it.

Daftar pendaftaran dengan nilai minimal:
A list of enrollments with a minimum score of 80 differs from the list of all enrollments. The condition determines which records are included in the result. Understanding comparison boundaries helps avoid answers that are almost correct but wrong for certain values.

## Comparisons and boundaries

WHERE selects records that satisfy the condition. `score >= 80` accepts 80, while `score > 80` does not. `=` compares equality; text uses single quotes. WHERE selects rows, it does not delete them.

## AND, OR, and parentheses

AND requires both conditions to be true. OR needs only one condition to be true. Use parentheses when combining the two so the intent is clear: `(course_id = 10 OR course_id = 20) AND score >= 80`.

## Evidence from source records

Separate the work: pick records with WHERE, pick columns with SELECT, then arrange the order with ORDER BY. Match each result to a single enrollment in the data object.

```sql
SELECT enrollment_id, score
FROM enrollments
WHERE score >= 80
ORDER BY enrollment_id;
```

## Reading condition boundaries

| score value | score > 80 | score >= 80 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 74 | No | No |
| 80 | No | Yes |
| 88 | Yes | Yes |

WHERE works on every source record. Records that do not meet the condition are not included in the result, but they remain stored. Conditions on text, for example `name = 'Alya'`, use text values in single quotes; column names are not written as text values.

## Summary

Comparisons set boundaries, AND requires all conditions to be true, and OR accepts either condition. Parentheses clarify combinations. SELECT picks columns; WHERE picks rows.

Pendaftaran nomor 6 dibatalkan. DELETE m:
Enrollment number 6 is cancelled. DELETE removes that enrollment record, not automatically the student or their course. The target and relationships that still reference the record must be considered before deletion.

## DELETE selects the record to delete

DELETE removes the record, it does not merely empty the score. Check `SELECT * FROM enrollments WHERE enrollment_id = 6;` then use the same PK predicate for DELETE.

```sql
DELETE FROM enrollments
WHERE enrollment_id = 6;
```

## Parent still referenced

Danu is students #4; enrollment #6 references him. Deleting students #4 first is rejected by the foreign key. There is no cascading delete in this dataset. Deleting enrollment #6 removes one relationship, not automatically Danu or his course.

## Confirm and restore the exercise

Preview shows the target record and the count that will be deleted. Once applied, the enrollment #6 object is gone and its related relationships disappear as well. Verify with SELECT, then Reset data to bring back the six enrollments.

## State before and after

| State | students | enrollments |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Before enrollment 6 is deleted | 4 records | 6 records |
| After DELETE succeeds | 4 records | 5 records |

Deleting a child record does not automatically delete its parent. Conversely, deleting the parent can be rejected while it is still referenced. Relationship rules must be read, not assumed. A DELETE without WHERE can wipe out every record in a regular database; the Quethink lab restricts this action to a single target.

## Summary

DELETE removes the record it targets. Keys and relations restrict deletion. Preview and verification support the decision, while reset only restores the local practice data.
